items.title: Live Updates: Hundreds of Thousands Join Another Round of Protests in France
items.summary: The interior ministry estimated that 320,000 people had demonstrated nationwide, a smaller number than the previous two Saturdays. The police and protesters clashed in Paris and other cities.
items.full_text: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Now, in cities across the country, antigovernment marchers are protesting expensive living conditions, high fuel prices and conditions in schools. Using the unrest as a smoke screen for vandalism, rioters and looters have also joined in . In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired rounds of tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration in the city, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people had demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes. Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening. There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform. The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020. The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall. “We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference. Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather in spite of the ban will lead to arrests, he said. Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration in which public order is disrupted. Here’s what else to know. Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people and inciting them to violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more › Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often end up in clashes with far-left groups. Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more › Giulia Imbert contributed reporting. But in an interview on YouTube, Mr. Macron said that social media platforms would be required “to remove illegal content, and to be very vigilant about the use of certain features to prevent them from being misused by people who want to engage in looting or other such activities.” That followed a report by a left-leaning online news site that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had sent a letter to leading telecommunications operators, asking them to be prepared to block Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Mr. Lecornu’s office declined to comment on the authenticity of the letter. Of the four reported recipients, one did not respond to questions and two declined to comment. A spokesman for the fourth, Orange, the only one in which the state is a shareholder, declined to confirm that a letter was received but said that “like any other operator, we are required to comply with the obligations legally imposed on us by the competent authorities, in accordance with applicable law.” With the protests in their second month, the police have arrested thousands, and politicians are divided over how to respond. Here is a breakdown of what has happened. Protest in a Parisian suburb Soon after returning from the summer break, students at a high school in the working class Parisian suburb of Créteil staged a protest, according to videos posted to social media on Sept. 18. The high schoolers objected to inadequate resources and high workloads. Within days, students elsewhere around Paris initiated similar demonstrations. At schools in the capital’s poorest suburbs, students blocked entrances to protest crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and what they say are flaws in the admissions system for higher education. Demonstrations spread across France By Sept. 29, the unrest had spread to around 400 schools around the country, according to rally organizers . The union of high school students said the blockades were a protest against a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.” Students barricaded the entrances to some schools with obstacles including e-bikes , while others threw projectiles and set fire to trash cans. The French education minister, Édouard Geffray, said that some of the students’ demands were “legitimate” but condemned the confrontational nature of their protests. He said that students had chased teachers and targeted school principals with firework-launching tubes. By the end of September, nearly 80 people had been injured, and the authorities had detained more than 440, including many minors. University students bolster the movement A sit-in by students blocking the street outside the Sciences Po university in Paris in early October. Credit... Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters Within days, the number of schools engulfed in the protests had doubled. According to the Interior Ministry , by Oct. 2, they had spread to more than 1,000 schools across France, including 220 that were blockaded. University students also began taking part. Around this time, the authorities said that the protests were mutating from legitimate expressions of educational grievances into something more dangerous, accusing people of shooting mortar-style fireworks, burning public buildings and looting. By Oct. 2, nearly 400 police officers and over 230 school employees and students had been injured. The number of arrests climbed to 3,000. The movement broadens The actions widened in October to encompass labor unions, parents and other activists, as different grievances converged into a mass protest. On Oct. 6, around 256,000 people marched through Paris and 40 other French cities, according to the Interior Ministry. A union of high school students said protesters had occupied some 1,800 high schools. The protests were mostly peaceful, but a fire was ignited in Lyon, and police officers used tear gas, including in Paris. The total number of arrested rose to 6,000, the authorities said. A major union of French judges and prosecutors and a human rights group accused the police of using disproportionate force , including against children as young as 14. Two days later , on Oct. 8, smaller demonstrations were staged throughout the country, rallying around 71,500 people. The following week, the Interior Ministry said that 160,000 people joined marches on Oct. 13 across France. The largest demonstrations yet More than half a million people joined 110 antigovernment marches throughout France on Oct. 17, according to an official estimate. A major union, the C.G.T., put the number even higher, at 800,000. Using either count, it was the largest day of protest since the demonstrations began in September. Many of the marchers were peaceful, but some were not. Around the country, rioters vandalized around 1,500 shops, the authorities said. In Paris, where over 100,000 people marched peacefully, a few hundred rioters faced off against officers. According to the police, the rioters burned cars and smashed storefronts . In the large town of Limoges, in central France, rioters set fire to the 19th-century City Hall. In a moment captured on video , the building’s spire collapsed in flames.

items.title: Hack Could Leave AO3, a Popular Fan Fiction Site, Offline for Weeks
items.summary: AO3, which hosts 18 million stories spun off from the likes of “Harry Potter” and “Heated Rivalry,” was taken offline after “an intrusion,” one of its founders said.
items.full_text:
Title: Hack Could Leave AO3, a Popular Fan Fiction Site, Offline for Weeks - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/arts/ao3-fan-fiction-site-down.html

Published Time: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 18:25:16 GMT

Markdown Content:
One of the world’s leading fan fiction websites, a repository of homespun stories based on works like “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry,”announced this week that it would be offline for maintenance for as long as a month.

Its members were stunned. The site, AO3, short for “Archive of Our Own,” houses 18.8 million works across 83,000 fandoms inspired by books, films and even celebrities, such as the members of K-pop bands. It is run entirely by volunteers, and operated by a nonprofit, the Organization for Transformative Works.

Rebecca Tushnet, a founder of the organization, said in an interview on Friday that there had been “an intrusion” on AO3 and that an all-volunteer crew was working to “figure out the path that the attacker used and make sure that it’s been removed.”

That was a day after AO3 said on its [Tumblr page](https://ao3org.tumblr.com/) that it had “detected evidence of a security incident.” It said it was still “determining its scope” but assured its 12 million users that no data had been lost. “All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe,” it said.

An outage of that duration is “nearly unheard-of,” Mark Graham, the director of the Wayback Machine, a digital repository operated through the Internet Archive, said in an email. He noted that a surge in traffic to archived versions of the site was now “putting a heavy load on the Wayback Machine,” which records snapshots of hundreds of sites daily across the internet.

[Mehdi Daoudi](https://www.logicmonitor.com/leadership?lmrd_id=try-it-free-cta&lmrd_variant=try-it-free-control&lmrd_session_id=1793370069812-0.13682050753364428), an expert on internet resilience at the infrastructure monitoring company LogicMonitor, said that there can be many reasons for a service disruption, but they typically last for only a few minutes to a few hours.

“When I see something like this,” he said, “I can only speculate that there is something major being rebuilt.”

Ms. Tushnet, a legal scholar at Harvard Law School, said “there was no reason to believe” that AO3’s database had been downloaded. The team is prioritizing safety over speed, she said, and will need two to four weeks maintenance to ensure “that we haven’t missed anything.”

“We’re aware that fan fiction plays a big role in fans’ lives,” she added, “and we are taking that seriously.”

In July 2023, AO3 was the target of a distributed denial-of-service attack, in which hackers flood the servers hosting a website until it becomes overloaded and shuts down. AO3 was offline for 28 hours. A hacker group called Anonymous Sudan claimed responsibility and said it had targeted the site for hosting explicit content and stories with L.G.B.T.Q.+ themes. AO3 said at the time that it urged “caution in believing any reasoning” proposed for such an attack.

Anne Jamison, an English professor at the University of Utah who teaches a course on fan fiction and who wrote the book “Fic: Why Fanfiction Is Taking Over the World,” said that part of the appeal of AO3 is the freedom it affords its members, unlike FanFiction.Net, an older site created in 1998 that is known for purging content.

Since its creation in 2009, AO3 has become “central to just a vast and multifaceted storytelling phenomenon,” she said.

“A lot of queer content, a lot of queer romance is on AO3,” Dr. Jamison said, adding that it can be the only content with gay themes available in countries where same-sex relationships are criminalized.

“So it can have a pretty important cultural function,” she added.

Dr. Jameson was up at 2 a.m. on Thursday looking for a reprieve from a grueling workweek when she visited the site and saw it was down.

“It’s like your library disappeared,” she said.

Many in the fan fiction community feel the same. Online, fan fiction devotees bemoaned the loss and swapped PDF downloads of stories. Users of Reddit have attempted to diagnose the outage in long threads on the website.

“I mean, people are so sad,” Dr. Jameson said, noting that the site receives hundreds of millions of views a week. “Like, I can’t even.”

She relayed a message from one of her students: “I have 18 tabs open on my browser from AO3, and I can’t believe I now have to be productive.”

Celeste Lavin contributed research.
